lesson.title: How a Curve Bends: Mapping Concavity from Start to Finish
lesson.summary: Sweeping the sign of the second derivative across a function's entire domain reveals every interval where the graph curves upward like a cup and every interval where it curves downward like a dome, explaining why the Second Derivative Test works.
lesson.body:
Concavity tells you something the first derivative cannot: not just whether a function is increasing or decreasing, but whether that increase or decrease is speeding up or slowing down. A function whose graph bends upward like the inside of a cup is concave up, and a function whose graph bends downward like the outside of a dome is concave down. Concavity analysis means doing for the second derivative exactly what local extrema analysis did for the first: sweeping across the whole domain to build a complete map of where each type of bend occurs, rather than checking concavity at a single point.

Continue the running example from local extrema analysis, f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 5, whose second derivative is f''(x) = 12x - 6. Solving f''(x) = 0 gives x = 1/2. Since f'' is linear it changes sign only once, so this single value splits the domain into exactly two intervals to test: (negative infinity, 1/2) and (1/2, positive infinity).

Testing a point in each interval: at x = 0, f''(0) = -6, negative, so the graph is concave down there. At x = 1, f''(1) = 6, positive, so the graph is concave up there. Putting that together, f is concave down on (negative infinity, 1/2) and concave up on (1/2, positive infinity).

This lines up exactly with the local extrema found earlier. The local maximum at x = -1 sits inside the concave down region, which makes sense: a true peak needs the graph curving downward around it, like the top of a dome. The local minimum at x = 2 sits inside the concave up region, which also makes sense: a true valley needs the graph curving upward around it, like the bottom of a cup. This consistency is exactly why the Second Derivative Test works at all. Checking the sign of f'' at a critical number is really just asking which way the curve bends there, and the bend alone tells you whether you found a peak or a valley, no separate sign chart needed on both sides.

Notice that x = 1/2, where the concavity switches, is not itself a critical number of f. Checking, f'(1/2) = 6(1/4) - 6(1/2) - 12 = 1.5 - 3 - 12 = -13.5, which is nowhere near zero. So x = 1/2 marks a change in how the curve bends, not a peak or a valley. Keeping these two ideas separate, where the graph turns around versus where it changes its bend, sets up the precise language needed for the next topic: inflection points.
